claims.text: The as-deposited coating has a dual-phase FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy microstructure.
The as-deposited coating initially has limited chemical ordering at its interphase boundaries.
The as-deposited coating contains deposition-induced defects.
Continuous loading dynamically develops short-range chemical order at FCC/BCC phase boundaries.
Dynamic interfacial short-range chemical order is the source of the coating's enhanced creep resistance.
Interfacial chemical ordering stabilizes FCC/BCC boundaries against deformation-driven diffusion.
Interfacial chemical ordering stabilizes FCC/BCC boundaries against dislocation motion.
Deposition parameters or post-deposition thermal treatments can be used to induce or suppress local chemical ordering at the phase boundaries.
Chemically ordered interphase-boundary regions act as pinning sites that impede dislocation mobility and boundary diffusion.
Increasing barriers to dislocation nucleation or migration can reduce creep progression.
Atomic diffusion and dislocation motion can be active creep-deformation mechanisms under sustained stress and elevated temperature.
The proposed ordering mechanism operates below conditions that cause additional phase transformations or dynamic recrystallization.
Coatings with enhanced interfacial short-range order will have lower steady-state creep strain rates than untreated coatings.
Coatings with enhanced interfacial short-range order will show a delayed onset of tertiary creep relative to untreated coatings.
Enhanced-order coatings will show reduced dislocation activity near phase boundaries.
Untreated as-deposited coatings with minimal interfacial order have higher creep rates and earlier tertiary creep despite similar overall plastic deformation.
